items.prompt: What is the passage mainly explaining?
options: Why the earliest wet period offers the best opportunity for the whole population
How soil prevents eggs from receiving water
How aquatic animals predict which wet period will last longest
Why delayed hatching can be useful in an unpredictable habitat
items.explanation: The passage explains the benefits and costs of spreading hatching across wet periods.
items.title: Life in a temporary pond
items.passage:
Some ponds contain water for only part of the year. They fill after rain and later shrink or dry out. For animals living in them, the disappearance of water is not merely an occasional emergency; it is a recurring feature of the habitat. Certain small aquatic animals survive these dry periods as resistant eggs, which remain in the soil until water returns.
It might seem that all such eggs should hatch as soon as the pond fills. However, a brief rain can create a pond that disappears before the young animals have time to reproduce. If only some eggs hatch during one filling, other eggs remain available for a later opportunity. This spreads the risk across different wet periods, rather than committing every potential offspring to the same uncertain event.
The strategy has a cost. An egg that stays dormant misses an opportunity if that particular wet period turns out to be long and favorable. The balance between immediate reproduction and waiting therefore depends on how predictable local conditions are.
Temporary ponds demonstrate that an apparently inactive stage can be an important part of an animal’s life cycle. Survival depends not only on what happens while water is present, but also on how a population persists between those periods.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a reference pitch?
options: To prove that historical music used incorrect frequencies
To remove differences between musical styles
To help musicians tune to a shared starting point
To make all instruments produce the same tone quality
items.explanation: A common reference supports coordination.
items.title: Why a musical pitch becomes a standard
items.passage:
Musicians playing together need a shared starting point for tuning. If two instruments use different reference pitches, a note with the same name may sound different on each. A standard pitch makes coordination easier, particularly when instruments and performers come from different places. Yet adopting a standard is not the same as proving that one frequency is uniquely correct for every musical purpose.
Instrument construction can make a change expensive. An instrument designed for one pitch level may not perform equally well at another, and some instruments cannot be adjusted very far. A new standard can therefore require replacement or modification of equipment. These costs help explain why older conventions may remain in use even when a different convention offers advantages for wider cooperation.
The choice is also affected by the music being performed. A group interested in recreating an earlier style may deliberately select a reference different from the one used by a modern orchestra. In that setting, difference is a goal rather than a failure to coordinate, provided that the participating musicians agree with one another.
A musical standard thus solves a practical problem of compatibility. Its success should be judged partly by whether it allows people and instruments to work together, not by whether it eliminates every alternative practice.

items.prompt: What is the passage’s main point?
options: Diagrams are useful mainly for communicating decisions after a design is complete
A clear diagram can establish connections before supporting evidence is gathered
Exhibition layouts should be drawn only after construction
Diagrams can aid reasoning but need to represent uncertainty
items.explanation: The passage balances the reasoning benefit with a caution about certainty.
items.title: Thinking with diagrams
items.passage:
A diagram is often treated as a simplified picture of something that already exists. In design work, however, it can do more than communicate a finished idea. Drawing boxes, arrows, or boundaries may help a person discover a relationship that was difficult to notice while considering the problem only in words.
Suppose a team is planning how visitors will move through a small exhibition. A written list can specify which displays are available, but a sketch can reveal that two groups will be directed toward the same narrow doorway. The drawing makes a possible conflict visible before the exhibition is built. It therefore contributes to the reasoning rather than merely illustrating its result.
This advantage also creates a danger. Once a relationship has been drawn neatly, people may treat it as more certain than the evidence warrants. An arrow might represent a tested connection or only a guess. If both are shown in the same way, the diagram hides an important difference. Designers can reduce this problem by using different marks for confirmed relationships and tentative ones.
Diagrams are most useful when people can revise and question them. Their power comes from making aspects of a problem easier to inspect, not from giving every line on a page the authority of an established fact.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of unit pricing?
options: To compare prices for equivalent quantities
To rank products by their overall quality
To eliminate differences in product concentration
To ensure that the largest package is always purchased
items.explanation: Unit pricing standardizes price by quantity.
items.title: Comparing prices by unit

stimulus.title: Comparing prices by unit
stimulus.script:
A larger package often looks like better value, but package size alone doesn’t tell us the cost of what we’re buying. Unit pricing expresses the price for a standard quantity, perhaps a hundred grams or one liter. It lets us compare products whose packages contain different amounts.
Suppose a small packet costs less in total than a large one. The large packet may still have a lower price per hundred grams. For someone who will use everything, that could be a saving. But if half of the larger packet is likely to be wasted, the lower unit price doesn’t necessarily mean a lower cost for the amount actually used.
There are other limits too. Products may differ in concentration, so an equal volume may not provide an equal amount of useful material. And two items that serve the same broad purpose may differ in quality or suitability. Unit pricing makes one comparison clearer; it doesn’t make every other consideration disappear.
The lesson is that a standard measure is a tool, not a decision made on our behalf. It helps answer a precise question about price and quantity. We still need to decide whether that question captures what matters in our particular situation, including storage, waste, and how we intend to use the product.

items.prompt: Why might a lower unit price fail to save a buyer money?
options: The buyer must purchase two packages at once
A smaller package always contains better material
Some of the larger purchase may not be used

items.explanation: Waste can offset the apparent quantity-based saving.

items.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How every new tree immediately changes local weather
Why surface temperatures cannot be compared
Why trees affect only the appearance of a street
The conditions that determine how street trees provide cooling
items.explanation: The talk explains mechanisms and the importance of placement and survival.
items.title: Trees and the temperature of a street

stimulus.title: Trees and the temperature of a street
stimulus.script:
On a warm day, two nearby streets can feel surprisingly different. Trees are one reason. Their leaves intercept sunlight, reducing the energy that reaches a pavement or a parked car. Shade can therefore change the temperature of surfaces that would otherwise absorb strong sunlight.
Trees also exchange water with the atmosphere. Water moves through the plant and is released from leaves as vapor. That process uses energy and can contribute to local cooling. But its extent depends on conditions such as water availability and the health of the tree. Planting a tree doesn’t immediately guarantee the same cooling effect in every street.
The location and shape of planting matter as well. A small new tree provides less shade than a mature one, and a tree placed far from where people walk may offer little direct protection to pedestrians. Underground space for roots can be just as important as the visible space above the ground.
So evaluating a street-tree program requires more than counting how many trees were planted. We need to ask whether they survive, develop useful cover, and improve conditions where people spend time. A planting count describes an action taken. A later assessment of shade and comfort tells us more about the result that action was meant to achieve.

It reduces the sunlight reaching the surface
It increases the amount of light reflected by leaves
items.explanation: Leaves intercept incoming solar energy.

items.prompt: What is the main point of the talk?
options: Animal communication can be studied without field conditions
A recorded signal must be interpreted in relation to its surroundings and measurement
A louder call is always more effective than a quieter one
Background noise affects instruments but not listeners
items.explanation: The talk links signal detection with context and measurement.
items.title: A signal against background noise

stimulus.title: A signal against background noise
stimulus.script:
Communication depends not only on producing a signal, but also on that signal standing out from its surroundings. Think about trying to hear a friend speak beside a busy road. Your friend may be speaking clearly, yet traffic noise can make the message difficult to distinguish.
Animals face a comparable problem. A call that travels well in one habitat may be less effective in another because vegetation, distance, and competing sounds affect what reaches a listener. Researchers therefore pay attention to the setting in which a call is produced, not just to the call recorded by itself.
Suppose a field recording contains a call that seems faint. That observation alone doesn’t establish that the animal produced a weak call. The microphone may have been far away or pointed in the wrong direction. A second recording made under known conditions can help separate the properties of the signal from the effects of recording it.
This distinction matters beyond animal communication. In many kinds of research, we observe a process through an instrument. The recorded result combines something about the source with something about the conditions of measurement. Careful comparisons make it easier to decide which part of the result belongs to the thing we want to understand.

The animal must have been unable to call normally

items.explanation: Distance is an alternative explanation for recorded faintness.

A second recording made under known conditions can help separate the properties of the signal from the effects of recording it.
This distinction matters beyond animal communication. In many kinds of research, we observe a process through an instrument. The recorded result combines something about the source with something about the conditions of measurement. Careful comparisons make it easier to decide which part of the result belongs to the thing we want to understand.

items.prompt: What is the value of a recording made under known conditions?
options: It removes the need to listen to the original recording
It guarantees that the animal will make a louder call
It helps distinguish source properties from measurement effects
It makes every habitat acoustically identical
items.explanation: Known conditions support a better interpretation of the result.
items.title: A signal against background noise

stimulus.title: A signal against background noise
stimulus.script:
Communication depends not only on producing a signal, but also on that signal standing out from its surroundings. Think about trying to hear a friend speak beside a busy road. Your friend may be speaking clearly, yet traffic noise can make the message difficult to distinguish.
Animals face a comparable problem. A call that travels well in one habitat may be less effective in another because vegetation, distance, and competing sounds affect what reaches a listener. Researchers therefore pay attention to the setting in which a call is produced, not just to the call recorded by itself.

items.title: Write an Email
items.subject: Suggestion for the project feedback session
items.scenario: Your class has a feedback session scheduled for its group projects. Several groups will present, and you are concerned that the current schedule leaves little time to discuss each project. You have an idea that could make the feedback more useful without extending the session. Write to the instructor.
points: Explain your concern about the current arrangement.
Describe your proposed change to the session.
Explain how the change would benefit the class and offer to help.

items.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
items.question: In a course where students learn a practical skill, should instructors give detailed step-by-step directions or allow students to discover methods through trial and error? What balance would you recommend, and why? Consider both the quality of learning and the difficulties students may face.
students: Clear directions should come first. Beginners can spend a lot of time repeating the same mistake without understanding it. Once they know a reliable method, they can try variations and compare the results.

I would allow more discovery. When students have to decide what to try, they become active problem-solvers. If the instructor explains every step in advance, students may finish the task without learning how to approach a new one.
